_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Tarba de’atma: the fat of the kidneys that lies on the thigh.
rashi:a1.2: Bemar dekhanta: [he sold it] as though it were permitted fat, which is called kanta (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), as in “the hadra dekhanta” that we mention in Shechitat Chullin (48b).
tosafot:a1.1: Tarba de’atma bemar dekhanta: this is how Rabbeinu Tam reads it. Mar means “in exchange for” kanta, as in “bemar deshechuta” in chapter Gid HaNasheh (Chullin 94a), and as in “bemar defarzela” in Bava Kamma (113b).
gershom:a1.1: Who would sell fat bemadkhanta: [a printed correction reads: he would sell fat of the thigh and say that it was permitted (“pure”); so it should read, and so it is in the Arukh, entry markanta.] [He passed it off as fat] that is permitted, of the hadura dekhanta; kanta means permitted, like “clean.” Our teacher told us, saying in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak HaOrlini, that the akashta and the aitra mentioned in Shechitat Chullin are fats of the abomasum, but the hadura dekhanta is entirely permitted.
gershom:a2.1: In accordance with whom? Rabbi Yehuda: who penalizes everything.
gershom:a3.1: If so, even water and salt too: he should penalize him for them. Why did he penalize him only for nuts?
rashi:a2.1: Actually, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: who penalizes only for something similar to the prohibition. And here it is the prohibition itself, for the thing with which he commits the prohibition, namely the nuts.
rashi:a2.2: Geru be’amguzei: are drawn and pulled after nuts.
rashi:a2.3: And misleads the butchers’ children: he leads them astray with nuts and hires the butchers’ children with them, and they bring him the fat, which they steal from their fathers, and he sells it as permitted fat.
gershom:a4.1: Actually, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon: who says, anything that has a connection [to the prohibition]; and these nuts too are connected to the prohibition.
rashi:a3.1: Mishna. Is not suspect with regard to tithes: so one may buy produce from him in the other years of the seven-year cycle, and need not tithe it as certainly untithed, only as demai. The reason for the whole mishna is explained in the Gemara.
gershom:a6.1: One who is suspect with regard to the Sabbatical Year: of selling it, for it is forbidden to sell [produce of] the Sabbatical Year.
rashi:a4.1: Gemara. Requires a wall: for one may eat second tithe only inside the wall of Jerusalem, as it is written: “And you shall eat before the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 14:23).
tosafot:a4.1: Tithes, which require a wall, are stringent for him: from here Rabbeinu Tam infers that wherever tithe is mentioned alongside the Sabbatical Year, it speaks of one who treats second tithe as non-sacred. For example: “These remain in their presumptive status with regard to tithes and the Sabbatical Year,” in chapter HaNizakin (Gittin 61b); and likewise, “he need not be concerned about the spices in it, neither due to the Sabbatical Year nor due to tithe,” in the first chapter of Chullin (6a). The word “tithe” also proves it, for where the concern is that the produce has not been tithed, the Talmud says tevel or demai.
gershom:a7.1: Since it is prohibited to him for trade and has no redemption: as we say, the last [item it is exchanged for] is caught up in the Sabbatical Year, and the produce itself remains prohibited.
gershom:a8.1: Since he is suspect regarding Torah law: that is, the Sabbatical Year and tithe; all the more so regarding rabbinic law.
gershom:a9.1: For [with] ritually pure items, eating non-sacred food in purity is only by rabbinic law.
rashi:a7.1: The ritually pure items: they are rabbinic, that a person should eat non-sacred food in purity.
rashi:a7.2: But one who is suspect: on ritually pure items is suspect on the Sabbatical Year.
tosafot:a7.1: But one who is suspect is suspect: [the Gemara draws this inference] because it holds that the statement itself was not needed, since it is obvious that one trusted on ritually pure items is trusted on the Sabbatical Year, as he conducts himself in the manner of the Perushim, who eat non-sacred food in purity.
gershom:a10.1: But: one who is suspect on ritually pure items is also suspect on the Sabbatical Year. And this is difficult for the mishna, which teaches: There are those suspect on ritually pure items who are suspect neither on this nor on that.
rashi:a8.1: The mishna: which teaches “is not suspect,” is where we saw him observing the law of tithes and the Sabbatical Year privately within his home. One cannot say he is doing it for show, since he does it privately.
tosafot:a8.1: In brief: The mishna is where we saw him observing [the Sabbatical Year] privately within his home. This implies that an ordinary am ha’aretz is suspect on the Sabbatical Year just as on ritual purity. Tosafot find this difficult from the end of HaNizakin (Gittin 61a): asked why the mishna there is lenient with the wife of an am ha’aretz but strict with a woman suspected about the Sabbatical Year, Rava answers that it speaks of Rabbi Meir’s am ha’aretz and of rabbinic impurity; since it says simply “am ha’aretz” about purity but “one suspected” about the Sabbatical Year, ordinary amei ha’aretz are suspect on purity but not on the Sabbatical Year. (The ruling there permitting sifting and grinding with an am ha’aretz suspect on impurity proves nothing, since it may speak of the other years of the cycle, or of produce known not to be Sabbatical, just as, according to Rava, who rejects Abaye’s answer that most amei ha’aretz tithe, it speaks of produce known to be tithed.) It is also difficult for Rabbeinu Tam’s explanation in Ketubot (24a), at “mine is new and my fellow’s is old,” that an ordinary am ha’aretz, though suspect on demai, is not suspect on the Sabbatical Year. [Rabbeinu Tam there] rejects Rabbeinu Shmuel, who explains “new and old” with reference to the Sabbatical Year and reads the answer “most amei ha’aretz tithe” as applying to the Sabbatical Year too, and he explains “new and old” as mere praise of the goods, not a matter of prohibition. Now, according to Rabbi Ilai, one suspect on rabbinic purity is suspect on the Sabbatical Year; all the more so ordinary amei ha’aretz, who, just as they are suspect on demai, which is Torah law, are suspect on the Sabbatical Year. And it is forced to explain every ordinary am ha’aretz who is not suspect on the Sabbatical Year as one seen observing it privately in his home. A further difficulty: the mishna in Demai (3:4), cited in HaNizakin (Gittin 61b), says one who brings wheat to a Samaritan miller or an am ha’aretz miller need not be concerned for tithe or the Sabbatical Year, implying that ordinary amei ha’aretz are suspect on the Sabbatical Year. Answer: the Sabbatical Year is mentioned there because of the Samaritan, or else it speaks of one who is certainly suspect. So too the case of buying a lulav from one’s fellow in the Sabbatical Year, where we say one does not hand Sabbatical-Year money to an am ha’aretz (Sukka 39a), and the case of giving one’s neighbor dough to bake or a pot to cook, where one need not be concerned for the leaven and spices in it on account of the Sabbatical Year or tithe (Chullin 6a): all of these speak of one who is certainly suspect. And if you ask how the Gemara in Chullin proves from that case that the Sages decreed on mixtures of demai, since perhaps one who is suspect is worse than an ordinary am ha’aretz regarding first tithe, as is evident at the end of HaNizakin (Gittin 61a) according to Abaye: one can say that according to Rava the challenge stands, for he does not treat it as more stringent. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a11.1: When we saw him observing: the stringency of the Sabbatical Year and tithe within his home.
rashi:a9.1: Rabbi Yannai said: the baraita from which we inferred “but one who is suspect [is suspect]” is where he had been suspect on both, the Sabbatical Year and ritually pure items, and he accepted on both that he would be careful about both of them.
gershom:a12.1: Rabbi Yannai said: actually, it is as the mishna says. And what is the reason of the baraita, from which it is inferred “but one who is suspect is suspect”?
gershom:a13.1: For example, where he was suspect on both: on ritually pure items and on the Sabbatical Year and on tithe, and he came before the Rabbis and accepted on both, and then he was again suspected on one. Therefore, since at first he was suspect on all of them and now he is again suspect on one, we say that he is suspect on all of them as well.
rashi:a10.1: This is the statement of Rabbi Akiva: that one suspect on the Sabbatical Year is not suspect on tithe.
gershom:a14.1: This is the statement of Rabbi Akiva, the unattributed: this anonymous mishna, which teaches “one suspect on the Sabbatical Year is not suspect on tithes,” is Rabbi Akiva.
rashi:a11.1: The Sabbatical Year is stringent for them: and since he is suspect on the Sabbatical Year, all the more so on tithes.
tosafot:a11.1: In brief: In Rabbi Yehuda’s locale the Sabbatical Year was stringent for them, and therefore [one suspect on it] is suspect on tithe. Tosafot ask: in the first chapter of Shabbat (17b) we say that with teruma, since one can do as Shmuel says, that a single grain of wheat exempts the whole pile, people are not suspected [of neglecting it]. So too with second tithe we should not suspect him, since one can do as Shmuel says, that consecrated property worth a maneh that was redeemed on a peruta’s worth is redeemed, and the same holds for second tithe. [Tosafot support this:] the She’iltot of Rav Aḥai states it explicitly of a fourth-year vineyard, that one redeems it on something small, and second tithe and fourth-year produce share one law everywhere, as they are derived from each other through “holy, holy” (Kiddushin 54b); and it seems permitted even ab initio, as with consecrated property in Arakhin (29a), where it is permitted nowadays, in the case of the man who devoted all his property. And when Gittin (65a) sets “how does one act cunningly with second tithe” in second tithe nowadays, which is rabbinic, it could have asked: nowadays, why is a stratagem needed to avoid the added fifth, when one can redeem a maneh’s worth on a peruta’s worth? Instead it rejects that with another objection: is there a Hebrew maidservant nowadays? And every day we redeem a fourth-year vineyard worth a maneh on a peruta’s worth. Tosafot answer that tithe is not comparable to teruma: sometimes one has no peruta at hand to redeem it on, or has only a little tithe, worth about a peruta, and does not want to give a peruta for it. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a15.1: And in Rabbi Yehuda’s locale the Sabbatical Year was stringent: and since he is suspect on the stringent one, he is also suspect on the lenient one.
rashi:a11.2: For a certain person who would call his fellow: in Rabbi Yehuda’s locale.
rashi:a11.3: Dayyara bar dayyarta: a convert, son of a female convert.
rashi:a11.4: Teitei li: may a good reward come to me, for I did not eat Sabbatical-Year produce like you. Some explain “Rabbi Akiva, the unattributed” by what we say in Sanhedrin, chapter Elu Hen HaNeḥenakin (86a): an anonymous mishna is Rabbi Meir, an anonymous baraita is Rabbi Natan [so Rashi’s text here], and all of them follow Rabbi Akiva. But that is not right, for in several places we say “Rabbi Menaḥem, the unattributed,” “Rabbi Shimon, the unattributed.” Rather, [it means that] many mishnayot in the Talmud are anonymous in accordance with Rabbi Akiva.
gershom:b1.1: Dayyora bat dayyorta: a convert, daughter of a female convert. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “daughter of”; the daf reads “son of.”]
rashi:b1.1: One suspect on tithe is suspect on the Sabbatical Year: and all the more so, one suspect on the Sabbatical Year is suspect on tithe.
rashi:b1.2: And who are the Sages? Rabbi Meir: who says below that one suspect on one matter is suspect on the entire Torah.
tosafot:b2.1: And the Rabbis say: He is suspected only with regard to that matter: according to Rabbi Ilai above, one suspect on ritually pure items is suspect on the Sabbatical Year, except where we saw him observing it privately. So what is said here, “he is suspected only with regard to that matter,” is not exact; it means that matter and what is like it, and it comes only to exclude the entire Torah.
rashi:b3.1: He is like a Jewish meshummad: and we do not say that he is a complete gentile, as though he had never converted.
rashi:b3.2: That if he betroths: a woman after he abandoned his faith, his betrothal is a betrothal.
gershom:b2.1: His betrothal is a betrothal: and she requires a bill of divorce.
rashi:b4.1: Matters of ḥaver status: the Tosefta in tractate Demai explains them: that he not give teruma or tithe to an am ha’aretz, that he not prepare his ritually pure food at an am ha’aretz’s, that he eat non-sacred food in purity, and that he tithe what he eats, what he sells and what he buys.
rashi:b4.2: A detail of the scribes: a rabbinic stringency.
gershom:b3.1: Except for one matter, he is not accepted: for we say, since he cannot keep that one matter, [he will certainly not keep the others either].
gershom:b4.1: Even one detail: this part of the baraita refers to the gentile who comes to accept all the words of the Torah. [A bracketed gloss in the text repeats: he will certainly not keep the others either.]
rashi:b5.1: Matters of Levite status: to sing, to serve and to be a gatekeeper.
rashi:b5.2: Among the sons of Aaron: this implies that he must observe every law of the sons of Aaron, [and only then] “he shall have the right thigh for a portion.”
rashi:b6.1: That he practices in private: before he accepted it in our presence, he was already conducting himself by the law of ḥaver status, so there is no reason to suspect him and say he is doing it for show.
rashi:b6.2: He is accepted: we treat him as a ḥaver and as trustworthy in all his affairs.
gershom:b5.1: If we saw him practicing privately within his home before this, he is accepted at once, and afterward he is taught.
rashi:b7.1: For hands [kenafayim]: that he wash his hands before eating and before touching foods of teruma, for hands are in second-degree impurity.
rashi:b7.2: For ritually pure items: for the stringencies of the other matters of purity, so that we treat his pure foods as fully pure, and his teruma may be eaten as pure teruma.
rashi:b7.3: He is accepted: for he is not leaving out a whole matter, since he accepts the washing of hands, and that is the essence of eating non-sacred food in purity.
rashi:b7.4: He has not accepted even for ritually pure items: for since he cannot keep the law of washing hands, which is an easy thing to do, all the more so the rest.
gershom:b6.1: One is accepted for kenafayim, for washing the hands: if he accepted upon himself to be careful not to eat without washing his hands, and in everything that requires washing the hands.
gershom:b7.1: Afterward he is accepted for ritually pure items: to eat non-sacred food in purity.
gershom:b8.1: He has not accepted even for ritually pure items: that is, we do not rely on him even for what he did accept, for we say: since he could not keep what requires washing the hands, all the more so the rest of purity.
rashi:b8.1: Until when is he accepted: for ḥaver status, so that we accept him at once and treat him as a ḥaver?
rashi:b8.2: For liquids, thirty days: if he took ḥaver status upon himself [and kept it] for thirty days, from then on we trust him with the purity of liquids, whose impurity is light, for the impurity of liquids is rabbinic, as in the first chapter of Pesaḥim (16b).
rashi:b8.3: For clothing: to treat his clothing as a ḥaver’s, for it says in tractate Ḥagiga (18b): the garments of an am ha’aretz have the status of midras for Perushim.
rashi:b8.4: Twelve months: if he took ḥaver status upon himself for twelve months.
rashi:b9.1: This would be among the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel: and it should be taught along with the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel in tractate Eduyyot (5:1), where we say six matters are among the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel. If this were so, this too should be taught there. Another version: “until when is he accepted” refers to what we said above, that if he first practiced privately within his home he is accepted at once; [the question is] how long he must first practice so that we accept him at once.
gershom:b9.1: Until when is he accepted: that is, how long must we see him being careful about purity for him to be accepted as trustworthy for ritually pure items?
gershom:b10.1: For liquids: for the purity of liquids, thirty days.
gershom:b11.1: For clothing: for the purity of garments, as we say: the garments of an am ha’aretz have the status of midras for Perushim, and so on.
rashi:b11.1: Because a ḥaver who accepted is not comparable: [a ḥaver who accepted it] himself is not comparable to the son of a ḥaver [who has it] through his father’s acceptance, for he has no acceptance of his own, only his father’s habit, and his father is certainly more careful. Another version: this “because it is not comparable” is the first tanna speaking to him: why do his children and household not need to accept? Because a ḥaver who accepted is not comparable to the son of a ḥaver whose father accepted, for the son of a ḥaver is not suspect. And in the Tosefta, tractate Demai, we read: for a ḥaver who went astray is not comparable to the son of a ḥaver who went astray.
gershom:b12.1: Because a ḥaver who accepted is not comparable [a printed note: it seems it should read “a ḥaver who accepted to the son of a ḥaver who accepted”]: this implies, and so on, that he must accept before three. Another version: “it is not comparable,” and so on, refers to the first tanna, which is why he said that his children and household, and so on. Another version: “a ḥaver who accepted is not comparable,” and likewise “who accepted,” means this: since you said that a ḥaver himself must accept before three, all the more so the son of a ḥaver must accept before three. Hence the first tanna, who says his children and household need not accept: although the ḥaver himself must accept before three, a ḥaver who is the son of an am ha’aretz is not comparable to the son of a ḥaver. For a ḥaver who is the son of an am ha’aretz did not learn it in his father’s house, and he must accept before three; but the son of a ḥaver, who is used to purity because it is practiced in his father’s house, need not accept before three.
rashi:b13.1: This mishna was taught: that even a Torah scholar must accept.
rashi:b13.2: Concerning ritually pure items: we do not read “in the order of Teharot”; rather, an incident happened to them with ritually pure items themselves, and the halakha was in doubt.
rashi:b13.3: The Sages sent: they sent a pair of Sages.
rashi:b13.4: He seated Sages of his own: some of his students who had accepted ḥaver status upon themselves; he seated them beside those messengers, and he himself stood to examine their question.
gershom:b13.1: This mishna was taught in the days of the son of Rabbi Ḥanina: that a Torah scholar must accept before three, for he would suspect even a Torah scholar regarding his ritually pure items unless they had accepted before three.
gershom:b14.1: He seated Sages of his own: some of his students, to guard his ritually pure items while he went to examine the matter.
rashi:b14.1: This one’s father, and so on: he said this in his anger, and it is not so.
tosafot:b14.1: This one’s father degraded our students [so Tosafot’s text; the daf reads “Torah scholars”]: regarding ritually pure items, as his son did.
rashi:b15.1: The honor of the elder: the father and the son.
rashi:b15.2: Silsul: a higher standard. Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus was a priest.
gershom:b15.1: They told him: [the students told] Rabbi Yehuda how he had treated them, that he did not want to trust them with his ritually pure items. Rabbi Yosei said to Rabbi Yehuda: Let the honor of the elder be left in its place; that is, do not suspect him of degrading Torah scholars.
gershom:b16.1: Rather, from the day the Temple was destroyed, the Sages [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads “priests”] adopted silsul, a stringency.
rashi:b16.1: In its presumptive status until it is disqualified: until they sell indigo dye [kela ilan] there as tekhelet.
rashi:b17.1: They must accept ḥaver status “battehilla”: so we read, and we do not read “kebattehilla” [as at first]. And in the Tosefta we read “battehilla,” that is, at the outset, before we treat them as ḥaverim. And although we said above that his children and household need not accept, here it is different, since at the time of the acceptance they were not with him, and one could say they keep to their former habits.
rashi:b17.2: They need not accept: if they come back under the authority of a ḥaver.
rashi:b18.2: Tax seals: tax collectors have seals, and when people pay them the tax they give the payer a seal so that a second tax collector will not demand it from him again.
